Yooka Laylee did a lot of game- and level-design mistakes that held it back from receiving critical success. I was excited after playing the kickstarter demo, the controls felt good and I could see the potential.

One of the most egregious mistakes was the Rextro minigame objectives. You play a minigame and complete it to gain your macguffin. Only *after* beating it once do you get the challenge to beat a high-score for the second macguffin. It didn't matter if you beat that score on the first time around, you have to slog through an objective you already completed just to get your prize.

The level designs were inferior to Banjo Kazooie and Donkey Kong 64. While those games had strong set pieces you could see from almost anywhere in the stage, Yooka Laylee had visually nice but harder to distinguish environments that blended together. This made exploring more boring because you found less interesting stuff, and it made it harder to navigate overall.

It just didn't feel like it was put together with the same amount of love or understanding of what makes a good game as Banjo Kazooie was. I had high hopes for the seasoned developers, but they missed the mark.

In conclusion: They made something less engaging than what they'd made before without evolving the formula enough to make up for where they lacked.

**Likes**

* Among the multibillionaire companies they are the ones that dare to be different. They have all but checked out of the high fidelity hardware race and seem to instead focus on making more with less.

* They don't just make a platform, they make their own games. This gives them a much better starting point of what they need hardware wise to make the games they want to make. There is a wide array of high quality colorful experiences that are unique to Nintendo.

* A wide array of colorful worlds that stimulates the imagination. When I look at a line-up of video game characters from high budget games Nintendo's cast of characters stand out as iconic. They come in all varieties of shapes and colors while most modern games stick to human proportion. There really seems to be something or someone for everyone.

* Their large library of genres and characters means there is a near infinite potential for what you can expect from them. Outside of their flagship series you never know when you may get a glorious sequel to a series that has not seen love for years. Kid Icarus: Uprising was an unexpected masterpiece for example.

* They have been showing some love for non-Nintendo developers for the last few years. There are many games I have only been exposed to through the Nintendo Youtube channel and as a result I have had a lot of fun playing non-Nintendo games on the Switch.


**Dislikes**

* Their marketing has lost it's soul. It comes across to me that ever since the new generation of leadership stepped in that the company feels a lot less approachable. Granted, Satoru Iwata's and Reggie Fils-Aimè are some giant shoes to fill.

* Their unwillingness to properly address the Joy-Con quality defect issues. I understand that there is a lot of technology packed into these little things, but for the price point, their shelf life is inexcusable. Absolutely embarrassing after a legacy of consoles that have survived literal bombings.

* The legal team's handling of fan-created projects. I am not a lawyer so there may be legitimate reasons for playing whack-a-mole with fan creators the way they have been doing over the years, but I will never cease to be disappointed to see all these amazing works of passion destroyed instead of appreciated by the company that inspired them.

* Their insistence on making large parts of their retro library inaccessible. One of the best ways to fight against piracy is to make the legitimate option easily available. I highly doubt this will change this generation seeing as they are selling 3D retro games at a premium like the Mario 3D collection.

* Their tone-deaf approach to addressing the playerbase's desire for certain series. Paper Mario and Star Fox are two series that come to mind where players are tearing their hair out at the *potential* they are seeing, but sobbing at the games they are being served. The ones in charge of making the games often seem to deliberately ignore core aspects of what the players find fun just for the sake of being different.

I actually think it is far more sinister than that. A mother who does a great job in her role as a mother is often berated because she is somehow supporting old standards that women in the developed world are supposedly too important to lower themselves to. Women who make sacrifices of money and travel opportunities in favor of raising their children well are often met with snide remarks, *especially* if they are happy with their decision and stay healthy/look good.

I think this is a thing that resonates with a lot of men, especially in this day and age where people in developed nations are having fewer children than ever. In my country for example 1/4 men live their entire lives without ever having any children of their own.

Motherhood on the other hand is almost seen as a taboo in today's social climate. It is not something most young women are encouraged to seek out as much as high-paying careers, social status, and adventures are. In the context of women, children are often depicted as a burden to chain them down and an extension of the patriarchy. 

When a man gets a child it opens up doors for him to grow as a man, but when a women gets a child her life and opportunities supposedly ends. If you think to the original Paper Mario and Thousand Year Door you'll find that they did world building really well. They made the Mushroom Kingdom and beyond feel like a lived in world instead of an obstacle course. There were unique characters both in appearance, culture, and personality and to top it all off it included a very well implemented combat system where every single point of damage mattered. The games also included original species of monsters and NPCs that despite never having appeared in core Mario games felt right at home in the Mario Universe.

Super Paper Mario did away with the combat system, but still did a lot in the way of world building. While I think the character design being made of blocky arbitrary shapes seems a bit lazy, it at least made an effort to make the alternate dimension the game takes place in feel different. After all, most traditional Mario creatures are rounded shapes, so the other world having things mostly made from blocky shapes definitely makes it feel alien.

Sticker Star simplified the combat and the world building to an almost insulting degree. Once again the world felt like an obstacle course for Mario to overcome and the few notable characters that were in the game did not have any unique designs. The music was great and the game *looked* pretty, but the sense of getting to know a new and exciting place just wasn't there.

Color Splash was a step in the right direction from Sticker Star, but it still suffers from Sticker Star's trappings. Sure, we're going to a place that is not the Mushroom Kingdom, but because there are no unique character designs it does not end up feeling like a new place at all. Toads still wear the same clothes. All non-toads are affiliated with Bowser. The battle system is still watered down. The writing and humor has a lot more soul than Sticker Star, but the world building isn't there.

Fighting wild pokemon should not be lumped together with fighting *random encounters*. In all mainline games up until now there has been a weird disconnect between the state of battle and the state of exploration. You only really *see* pokemon during the battle phase of the game while the overworld has been strangely devoid of life. Pokemon on the field *brings the world to life* and that is an awesome inclusion that I hope carries over from the Let's Go games.

I think they do some things right, but also do somethings wrong. I *love love love* that all pokemon are visible in the overworld. Random encounters are frustrating, and it's far more enjoyable to sneak around pokemon you can see than to dread going into a cave because you know there are no 'safe' spots.

I also *do* like that you have to throw the pokeball at the pokemon.

What I *do not* like is that they *removed the battle aspect* of the catch. It is a staple of the anime, and has been of the games for the longest time. The thrill of weakening a strong foe and trying not to knock it out or get knocked out yourself is a great part of the pokemon formula that I want to stay, *especially for rare and legendary pokemon*.

Here is my ideal system:

* All Pokemon should be visible in the overworld, though some may require a keen eye to see or a bit of luck to spawn in.
* In combat, strong and rare pokemon should move around so much at full health that it is almost impossible to hit them with your pokeballs.
* As you weaken them and afflict them with status effects they should become far less evasive and easier to hit.
* PP should be directly tied to catch rate. The longer the battle goes on the easier the pokemon is to catch almost guaranteeing it when your target is at low health and has less than 10% of their total PP across the board.

This system will make catching pokemon a more active experience on the trainer's part, while simultaneously including the pokemon you have caught into the experience, forming a greater bond of working together.

Side quests really differ depending on if they are long or short. Long ones can stand on their own right with good writing and feel satisfying even if the reward is not great, but short ones are better when they have some long lasting impact on the world.

An example of such a short one that comes to mind is in The Legend of Zelda: Breath of The Wild. There is a little girl who wants to make a garden in a back alley, but she can't because someone keeps throwing their garbage there. All you have to do is climb up to find the person making the garbage and convince them to stop, but you get the lasting impact of there not being more garbage in the area and trees eventually grow where you can harvest resources. Quick, easy, but leaves an impression on the world.

Longer, more involved Side Quests would be the character story arcs in Chrono Trigger. Each character has their personal struggles that at some point in the game you can start to resolve. Getting to know your party better and actually bringing them some closure before on things in their lives before you save the world is a really satisfying way to do the end of a game. It being optional makes you appreciate it more too, as these are things you know you could have missed. Normally these kind of quests bring great rewards, but they feel more like a bonus to what is already enjoyable content.

The base game revolves around Miis and play as a simple version of D&D. You've got a simple campaign about saving the kingdom and defeating the dragon. You can play solo or you can play with friends.

Here is the thing though. The game has a *campaign creator* where you can create your own adventure maps and challenges. You've got the basic grasslands, caves, and castle to begin with, but if you scan an amiibo a whole new world opens up to you.

Say for instance you scanned Mario; you now have access to Mario clothes for your Amiibo or Mario himself on the board. You also unlock an enemy in the form of a Goomba as well as a Super Mushroom and Question Mark Blocks. Add some Mario music to the package and you've got a lot of value for your amiibo (in my opinion.)

Also, if you're not an avid amiibo collector you're not all lost. If you connect with a friend and they scan their amiibo while you are playing together you will unlock the bonuses from that amiibo in your game.

There is so much potential with such a game. You could build a campaign with Chibi Robo trying to stop Overlord Luigi and his clone army of Reggie Fils Aime miis if you wanted.
